practicalQuestion: How should symptoms, strength, movement quality, and sport-specific running or cutting exposure be combined when deciding whether to advance a collegiate athlete from individual rehabilitation to modified team practice?

decisionContext.population: Collegiate athlete returning after a lower-extremity injury
decisionContext.phase: Individual rehabilitation to modified team participation
decisionContext.outcome: Organize a transparent progress-or-hold decision using several relevant signals
decisionContext.constraints: Signals may be collected on different days; team demands vary; medical decision authority remains with the care team

evidenceConfidence.rationale: No source tests a combined decision rule for moving from individual rehabilitation to modified team practice against later outcomes. The most direct evidence is a 100-player case series and a single case report, both in male soccer players after ACL reconstruction. The rest is a systematic review of mostly ACL return-to-sport testing studies at moderate to severe risk of bias, a hamstring expert consensus, a narrative review on asymmetry and a 10-athlete Lisfranc series. Several included studies found that passing symmetry-based criteria did not identify who later reinjured. Sources also read asymmetry measures differently.

dimensions.sourceReview: Every claim is checked against the full original source text. The sources are a 100-player case series, a single professional case report, a systematic review of 114 return-to-sport testing studies, a hamstring expert consensus abstract reproduced in a research digest, and a narrative review abstract on asymmetry reproduced in a digest. The last is a 10-athlete Lisfranc case series. Several claims from the systematic review rely on its one-line table summaries of individual included studies, not on those original studies.
dimensions.directness: Indirect. Sources describe on-field rehabilitation stages, partial team sessions and individual tests. None evaluates how symptoms, strength, movement quality and running or cutting exposure should be weighted together at this transition, and none tests entry criteria for modified practice.
dimensions.consistency: Sources broadly agree that progression should be criteria based, multi-signal and symptom aware. On asymmetry, the case report paused running when a step asymmetry relative to the player's pre-injury baseline appeared alongside knee pain. A narrative review on asymmetry in sport generally reports that asymmetry measures fluctuate and correlate poorly. One included study found limb symmetry did not change after injury because both limbs declined. Several included studies found that passing symmetry-based criteria did not identify later second ACL injury.
dimensions.transferability: Weak for this context. The most direct sources are male soccer players after ACL reconstruction, and the case series authors say their findings likely do not apply to female players. The review includes mixed-sex and some collegiate ACL studies, but at clearance testing rather than this transition. Hamstring and Lisfranc evidence is injury specific, and hip and ankle testing evidence in the review is sparse.

bottomLine.text: The evidence supports using several signals together rather than one test, but it does not tell you how to weight them. Published on-field programs combine movement quality, conditioning, sport skills and load. They advance using how the tissues respond together with defined stage criteria. In one series, even the final on-field stage did not fully prepare players for team training, especially for deceleration, and the authors call for modified training before full team integration. No study tested entry criteria for that step. No standardized return criterion exists, and in several studies passing symmetry-based tests did not identify who later reinjured. Treat any local rule as a transparent structure for care-team judgment, not a validated cut point.

actions.title: Option A: Staged on-field framework
actions.text: Use a staged on-field program in which each stage has defined criteria, and advance by comparing drills against how the knee and soft tissues respond. One 100-player soccer ACL series had no control group. In its final stage, workloads matched or exceeded team training for total, high-intensity and acceleration distance. Peak speed reached only 88% and deceleration distance 48%. Total distance plateaued, and the authors judged it not useful for progression decisions. Players who reached the last stage had higher return to competition rates, but the authors could not say whether workload, level of play or session number explained this.

actions.title: Option B: Capacity and symptom progression
actions.text: Progress on capacity and symptoms, with pain thresholds that depend on the activity and pain-free criteria for sprinting. This comes from an expert consensus on hamstring injuries. Symptom-led holds also appear in the ACL case report. There, knee pain delayed return to running, and a later step asymmetry with knee pain led to a short running pause. In a Lisfranc series, athletes returned to sport after regaining almost full plantar flexion strength and a pain-free single limb heel raise. A review also summarizes a hip arthroscopy surgeon survey that favored pain-free sport movements before return.

actions.title: Build the signal panel from separate domains
actions.text: Record strength, hop performance and movement quality as separate signals. In one included study, movement quality did not correlate with hop limb symmetry. Single leg hop for distance has low sensitivity on its own. Hop tests can give higher symmetry values than isokinetic strength testing. After injury, hop distance can fall in both limbs, so symmetry looks unchanged. Authors favor quadriceps strength testing. Handheld dynamometry has been validated against isokinetic testing, and in a healthy sample fixing the dynamometer improved reliability. One ACL case report used hamstring strength benchmarks to guide running speed: above 70% isometric strength to run above 15 km/h, and above 90% to run above 20 km/h. The report does not state what these percentages are relative to.

actions.title: Use modified practice for what individual rehab cannot supply
actions.text: High mechanical work intensities were hard to reach during individual on-field rehabilitation. Some football movements, such as cutting and decelerating, happen only with teammates and opponents, especially in competition. The ACL series authors call for further training, such as modified training, before full team integration. They cite their framework's suggestion that the last stage can be done as modified training with the team. In the later return-to-train phase, the case report describes partial team sessions, where the player joins only some drills or plays small-sided games as a floater. In one included study, a return to sports bridge program before unrestricted sport was reported to reduce knee reinjury. Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): plan modified practice as the next exposure step for cutting and deceleration, with the care team setting limits.

monitoring.label: Symptoms and tissue response
monitoring.text: Log pain and knee or soft-tissue response after each running or cutting session. Published frameworks use tissue response together with stage criteria to drive stage changes, and in the case report knee pain delayed and later paused running.

monitoring.label: Strength trend
monitoring.text: Track quadriceps strength and, where relevant, hamstring strength over time with a consistent method such as handheld dynamometry. In a healthy sample, a fixed setup improved reliability. The hamstring expert panel did not reach agreement on strength benchmarks, so treat any local threshold as provisional.

monitoring.label: Asymmetry with caution
monitoring.text: If you track step or limb asymmetries, compare them with the athlete's own pre-injury baseline and read them alongside symptoms. In the case report, a clear asymmetry relative to the pre-injury baseline coincided with knee pain. Both resolved on a softer pitch. A narrative review on asymmetry in sport reports that asymmetry measures are task and metric specific and fluctuate in magnitude and direction over time. Limb symmetry can also stay unchanged when both limbs decline. Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): note the collection date with each signal, because readings taken on different days may not agree.

guardrails.text: This brief informs criteria and monitoring only. Progression to modified team practice and any clearance decision stay with the treating clinicians and care team, working with performance staff.

Do not treat any single test or threshold as a clearance rule. No standardized return criterion exists. In several included studies, passing symmetry-based criteria or having more symmetric strength did not identify who later had a second ACL injury. Cleared collegiate athletes in one study still showed reduced triple hop symmetry.
Do not apply soccer ACL workload findings directly to female athletes. The 100-player series authors state their findings are most likely not applicable to female players.

limitations.text: The most direct sources are a case series of 100 male soccer players after ACL reconstruction and a single professional male case report. Neither tests a decision rule against a control group.

The return-to-sport testing review is dominated by knee and ACL studies, most at moderate to severe risk of bias. Its authors state that the included tests relied on limb symmetry or comparison with other metrics and were not followed for reinjury after clearance. However, some included studies did report second ACL injuries.
Symptom guidance comes from a hamstring injury consensus, a 10-athlete Lisfranc series and a hip surgeon survey, so transfer to other injuries is uncertain.
Several statements rely on the review's one-line summaries of individual included studies rather than the original studies.

whatCouldChange.text: Studies that follow collegiate athletes, including women, after a multi-signal progression decision and report reinjury or setbacks in modified practice.
Evidence showing whether asymmetry measures add value beyond strength and symptoms when deciding phase progression.

evidenceTension.text: The case report compared step impulse asymmetries from GPS-embedded sensors with the player's pre-injury baseline and read them alongside knee pain. Its authors describe them as useful for guiding phase progression. A narrative review on asymmetry in sport reports that asymmetry measures are task, metric and individual specific, fluctuate in magnitude and direction over time, and correlate poorly with each other. It also notes that injuries tend to accentuate asymmetries. In one included study, limb symmetry stayed unchanged after injury because both limbs declined. Several included studies found that symmetry-based criteria did not identify later second ACL injury.

claims.text: In a case series of 100 male soccer players after ACL reconstruction, a 5-stage on-field rehabilitation program implemented movement quality, physical conditioning, soccer-specific skills and training load. Stage transitions were driven by comparing drills, how the knee and soft tissues responded to loads, and defined stage-specific criteria.

evidence.excerpt: in which 4 important elements (movement quality, physical conditioning, soccer-specific skills, and training load) of a high-quality OFR approach were implemented.

The stage-to-stage transition was driven by a continuous comparison between different drills subjected to the player and the way the knee and soft tissues responded to the given loads along with defined stage-specific criteria.

claims.text: That study is a level 4 case series. 97 players had at least 9 months of follow-up. 84% returned to competition (100% of professionals and 80% of amateurs), and 10 players had an ACL reinjury.

evidence.excerpt: Study Design: Case series; Level of evidence, 4. Methods: OFR measurements/activities, global positioning system (GPS), and heart rate data were collected from 100 male 11-aside soccer players

A minimum 9-month follow-up was possible for 97 players (97%), with a median time of 2.3 years after ACLR and 84% RTC, with higher rates in professionals (100%) than amateurs (80%). Ten (10%) players sustained an ACL reinjury.

claims.text: In that series, typical external workload in the final on-field stage reached 106% of team training demands for total distance, 104% for high-intensity distance, 88% for peak speed, 110% for acceleration distance and 48% for deceleration distance.

evidence.excerpt: Typical external workload outputs in the final OFR stage aligned with team training demands for the total distance (TD) (106%), high-intensity distance (HID) (104%), peak speed (PS) (88%), acceleration distance (ACC) (110%), and deceleration distance (DEC) (48%),

claims.text: The authors of the 100-player male soccer series state their findings are most likely not applicable to female players returning after ACL reconstruction.

evidence.excerpt: Given the different training13 and match demands22,25 of women’s soccer, our findings are most likely not applicable to female players returning to soccer after ACLR

claims.text: The case report covered one professional male soccer player after ACL reconstruction. High mechanical work intensities were challenging to reach during individual on-field rehabilitation. The authors attribute this mainly to football movements that happen only when interacting with teammates and opponents, especially during competition, such as cutting, decelerating and ball interactions.

evidence.excerpt: reaching high mechanical work intensities are challenging during the individual on-field rehabilitation phases - this is mainly related to the specificity of some football movements that happen only when interacting with teammates and opponents, especially during competition (e.g., cutting, decelerating, ball interactions).

claims.text: In that case report with a hamstring graft, the authors describe hamstring strength as an important but not unique criterion for speed progression. Citing earlier work, they used isometric and eccentric benchmarks to guide run-based conditioning. Examples were above 70% isometric strength to run above 15 km/h, above 90% to run above 20 km/h, and above 90% eccentric strength for near-maximal speeds and change of direction. The report does not state the reference for these percentages.

evidence.excerpt: Hamstring strength is believed to be an important (but not unique) criterion for speed progression14; we used isometric and eccentric benchmarks to guide the run-based metabolic conditioning programming
>70% isometric strength to run >15 km/h - Type 1 & 3 run-based HIIT with work/rest ratio >1, >90% to run >20 km/h
and >90% eccentric strength to reach speeds close to max and maximal change of direction intensities

claims.text: In that case report, transient episodes of knee pain after meniscus surgery delayed the return to running.

evidence.excerpt: In the present case, transient episodes of knee pain (as a consequence of the meniscus surgery) delayed the return to running

claims.text: The case report authors state that GPS-embedded inertial sensors add sport-specific information on stride mechanics and step impulse asymmetries, in addition to usual strength and mechanics assessments. They say this information can be used to guide phase progression and day-to-day programming.

evidence.excerpt: In addition to usual assessments of lower limb strengths and mechanics (e.g., force trace during jumps on force plates)

GPS-embed inertial measurement unit and associated analytics (e.g., ADI software) add invaluable sport-specific information to monitor stride mechanics and step impulse asymmetries throughout the rehabilitation process, that can be used to guide phase progression and day-today programming

claims.text: The case report authors emphasize continuous and parallel collaboration within the multidisciplinary team during late return-to-sport phases.

evidence.excerpt: we need to emphasize the continuous and parallel collaboration that is always required within the multidisciplinary team.

claims.text: An international expert consensus on hamstring injuries, reported in a research digest, recommends progressing rehabilitation on capacity and symptoms. Pain thresholds depend on the activity, except that pain-free criteria are supported for sprinting (85.5% agreement). Experts focus on match-play demands and capacity when setting the end goal and timing of return (89.8%).

evidence.excerpt: This panel recommends rehabilitation progress based on capacity and symptoms, with pain thresholds dependent on activity, except pain-free criteria supported for sprinting (85.5%).
Experts focus on the demands and capacity required for match play when deciding the rehabilitation end goal and timing of RTS (89.8%).

claims.text: In the same hamstring consensus, benchmarks for strength (66.1% agreement) and flexibility (40%) did not reach the consensus threshold.

evidence.excerpt: Benchmarks for flexibility (40%) and strength (66.1%) and adjuncts to rehabilitation (68.9%) did not reach agreement.

claims.text: A systematic review of 114 lower-extremity return-to-sport testing studies found no standardized criterion for return-to-sport clearance. 85% of studies addressed knee pathology and 82% ACL reconstruction. Only 6.2% addressed hip pathology and two addressed ankle injuries. Most included studies had moderate to severe overall risk of bias.

evidence.excerpt: Even with the enormous amount of literature that exists regarding ACL injuries and testing there is no standardized criterion for RTS clearance.
Eighty five percent of articles discussed RTS for individuals with knee pathology. Furthermore, 82% specifically analyzed RTS following ACL reconstruction.
Only 6.2% of studies analyzed RTS for individuals with hip pathology and only two studies analyzed RTS for patients with ankle injuries.
the majority of study’s overall bias was identified as moderate to severe with significant concerns for potential confounding bias as well as bias in selection of study participants

claims.text: The review authors state that the tests in their search used limb symmetry index or were validated against another metric. They state that none of the tests followed athletes after return-to-sport clearance to assess reinjury rates.

evidence.excerpt: Specifically, all the tests in this search used limb symmetry index or ‘‘validated” the test against another metric (ie. Hop test related to strength,) but none of them followed athletes once given RTS clearance to assess re-injury rates.

claims.text: One study summarized in the review found movement quality did not correlate with limb symmetry from jump tests and concluded movement quality should also be evaluated in return-to-sport testing.

evidence.excerpt: Quality of movement indicated no correlation with LSI from jump tests, therefore movement quality should also be evaluated in RTS tests.

claims.text: The review reports that most authors view quadriceps strength as vitally important. It also reports that several studies validate handheld isometric dynamometry against isokinetic testing, which is unavailable in most clinics.

evidence.excerpt: Majority of authors agree that quadriceps strength in particular is of vital importance. Because the gold standard (iso-kinetic testing) not being available in most clinics, several studies validate the use of handheld isometric dynamometry against isokinetic.

claims.text: The review reports that single leg hop for distance has low sensitivity for limb asymmetry when used alone, though it correlates strongly with knee extensor strength.

evidence.excerpt: The SLHD demonstrates low sensitivity when used in isolation while attempting to identify limb asymmetry prior to RTS; however, it does have a strong correlation with knee extensor strength.

claims.text: A narrative review of bilateral asymmetry in sport generally, reported in a research digest, makes three points. Asymmetry assessments are task, metric, individual and sport specific. They fluctuate significantly over time in magnitude and direction. They correlate poorly with each other and with general performance. It also notes that injuries tend to accentuate asymmetries, while pre-existing asymmetries have not been shown to increase injury risk.

evidence.excerpt: Assessments of bilateral asymmetries are highly task-, metric-, individual-, and sport-specific; fluctuate significantly in time (in magnitude and, more importantly, in direction); and tend to be poorly correlated among themselves, as well as with general performance measures.
While injuries tend to accentuate bilateral asymmetries, there is no evidence that pre-existing asymmetries increase injury risk.

claims.text: In a small case series of athletes after surgical fixation of ligamentous Lisfranc injuries, patients returned to sport once they had regained almost full ankle plantar flexion strength and could perform a single limb heel raise without pain.

evidence.excerpt: patients were able to return to sport when they had regained almost full ankle plantar flexion strength and perform a single limb heel raise without pain.

claims.text: In the 100-player series, deceleration distance after on-field rehabilitation was 48% of training and 26% of match play demands. The authors conclude that players were underprepared for the deceleration demands of soccer.

evidence.excerpt: the DEC distance was markedly shorter than the ACC distance in our study (ACC: 110% of training and 63% of match play; DEC: 48% of training and 26% of match play), indicating that players are underprepared for the DEC demands of soccer after OFR.

claims.text: In that series, total distance plateaued across stages, and the authors conclude it is not a useful metric for return decisions or for progressing through on-field rehabilitation.

evidence.excerpt: The plateau in TD suggests that it is not a useful metric for RTC decision-making or for progressing through OFR.

claims.text: The series authors conclude that on-field rehabilitation helped prepare players for return to team training but did not fully prepare them for full team training workloads. They highlight the need for further training, such as modified training, before full team integration.

evidence.excerpt: this study showed that OFR facilitates RTT preparation but does not fully prepare the players for the workload demands of full team training.

Only some metrics were restored with respect to team training, highlighting the need for further training (eg, modified training) before full integration with the team training practices and before RTC.

claims.text: The series authors cite the framework's developers, who suggest that the final stage reflects training simulation. It can be done in a controlled on-field setting or as modified training with the team.

evidence.excerpt: Buckthorpe et al10 suggest that the stage 5 activity of their OFR framework reflects training simulation and can be performed in a controlled environment (eg, OFR) or as part of modified training with the team.

claims.text: In that series, the 33% of players who reached stage 5 had higher return to competition rates than the rest (90% vs 71%). The authors state it remains unclear whether workloads, level of play or number of sessions explained this.

evidence.excerpt: Players who reached stage 5 of the OFR program (33%) had higher RTC rates compared with the rest of the cohort (90% vs 71%; P = .016).

it remains unclear whether increased OFR workloads enhanced physical and psychological readiness for RTC or whether it was the level of play or the number of OFR sessions that determined higher RTC rates.

claims.text: For the later return-to-train and return-to-competition phases, the case report describes progressively introducing the player into team sessions while still managing his own load. In these partial training sessions, he joins only some drills or plays small-sided games as a floater.

evidence.excerpt: progressively introducing the player into team sessions while still managing his own load - this often refers to “partial training sessions” (e.g., the player takes only part in some but not all drills of the session, plays small-sided games but as a floater)

claims.text: In the case report, step impulse symmetry showed a clear period of asymmetry relative to the pre-injury baseline after the return to running. This coincided with right knee pain and required a few days without running. When running resumed on a softer pitch, both the pain and the asymmetry disappeared.

evidence.excerpt: in comparison to pre-injury baseline step impulse symmetry during straight-line running, there was a clear period when returning to running when the left side was unloaded (or the right side, overloaded)
This asymmetry was associated with reported right knee pain and required the player to stop running for a few days.
and while running on a softer pitch, both the pain and the asymmetry disappeared.

claims.text: The case report authors recommend regularly monitoring fitness, range of motion, strength and running mechanics during the season, so that practitioners have reference points if an injury occurs.

evidence.excerpt: It is important to regularly monitor various indices of cardiovascular fitness, ROM, strength, and running mechanics during the season so that when an injury occurs, practitioners can have reference points toward which they can direct the rehabilitation process.

claims.text: The review's table summaries of individual included ACL studies do report second injury findings. In one study, patients with graft failure had greater and more symmetric quadriceps strength at return to sport than those without a second injury. In another, confident young athletes were more likely to meet all criteria but also more likely to sustain a second ACL injury. In a third, jump landing, hop and hamstring strength criteria failed to identify patients at risk of a second ACL injury.

evidence.excerpt: Pts with ACLR graft failure had greater and more symmetric quad strength at time of RTS compared with pts with no secondary injury.
more likely to meet al. l RTS criteria but also more likely to sustain a 2nd ACL injury after RTS
Better jump landing patterns, hop performance and greater hamstring strength greater likelihood for RTS, but these criteria failed to identify patients are at risk for 2nd ACL injury

claims.text: One ACL study summarized in the review reports that adding a return to sports bridge program before release to unrestricted sport improved outcomes. It also reduced ipsilateral knee reinjury and contralateral knee injury rates.

evidence.excerpt: Supplementing primary ACL reconstruction and standard physical therapy with a return to sports bridge program prior to release to unrestricted sports performance was effective at improving patient outcomes and decreasing ipsilateral knee reinjury and contralateral knee injury rates

claims.text: The review summarizes a survey of surgeons from high-volume hip arthroscopy centers. In it, 85% recommended that patients be able to perform all sport motions without pain, and a majority favored including pain-free running, jumping, lateral agility drills and single-leg squats.

evidence.excerpt: 85% of surgeons recommended patients need to be able to produce all motions involved in their respective sport without pain and a majority of surgeons agreed pain-free running, jumping, lateral agility drills, and single-leg squats should be included

claims.text: Two studies summarized in the review show limits of limb symmetry. In one, after a lower extremity injury, single leg hop distance declined in both the injured and uninjured limbs, so limb symmetry did not change. In another, hop tests gave higher limb symmetry values than isokinetic strength testing.

evidence.excerpt: Following a lower extremity injury, single-leg hop for distance performance degrades not only for the injured limb but also the uninjured limb. However, limb symmetry did not change following a lower extremity injury.
encouraged use of isokinetic testing with RTS as they provide significantly lower LSI values than hop testing

claims.text: The review reports one study of collegiate athletes after ACL reconstruction who had been cleared to return to sport. They still showed reduced triple hop limb symmetry.

evidence.excerpt: Another study with collegiate athletes who had undergone ALCR and have been cleared to RTS, found there is reduced THD LSI even in the cleared athletes

claims.text: In one study of healthy participants summarized in the review, fixing the handheld dynamometer with the person supine increased the reliability and validity of quadriceps strength measurement.

evidence.excerpt: Fixation of HHD during measurement in the supine position increases the reliability and validity in measuring the quadriceps strength

assumptions: The specific injury was not stated, so evidence centered on ACL reconstruction was used as the closest available model for a lower-extremity injury.
Modified team practice was taken to mean a step between individual on-field rehabilitation and full team training.
coverageGaps: No study tests a combined symptom, strength, movement quality and exposure rule for advancing from individual rehabilitation to modified team practice against later outcomes.
No tested entry criteria for modified or partial team practice. The sources describe this step but do not evaluate when to start it.
No collegiate or female cohort studied at the move from individual rehabilitation to modified team practice. The collegiate and mixed-sex evidence in the review comes from clearance testing.
Return-to-sport testing evidence for hip and ankle injuries is sparse. Other direct evidence covers only ACL reconstruction, hamstring injury and a small Lisfranc series.
No guidance on reconciling signals collected on different days.
